# R workshop 1:<br>Getting started in R and data handling

## Introduction

### What are R and RStudio?

R is the name of the programming language, while RStudio is an environment for working with R - essentially RStudio provides a user-friendly interface that makes writing, running, and managing R code much easier.

### Why R?

- Built specifically for data analysis and statistics
- Free and open-source
- Powerful tools for handling and analysing data
- Produces publication-quality graphs
- Widely used across scientific research disciplines
- A valuable skill for both further study and future careers

While many of the tasks covered in these workshops could be completed in other software such as Excel, the coding skills you develop will form the basis for conducting more advanced analyses in R and other statistical software.

## Workshop 1 overview

In the first workshop, you will learn how to navigate the RStudio interface, create and edit scripts, and run basic R code.

Some more specific learning outcomes are given below - this may look like a lot, but most of these are small skills that fit together to help you become confident using the basics of R and RStudio.

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
### [{{< fa regular lightbulb >}}]{style="color: #872046;"}  Learning outcomes

By the end of this session, you should be able to:

- Navigate the RStudio interface
- Understand the purpose of a script and how to create and save one
- Write and run R code from a script
- Write R commands to perform simple arithmetic calculations
- Understand the purpose of comments and how to write them in R
- Distinguish between expressions and assignments
- Use the correct syntax to assign numeric vs. character values to objects
- Refer to stored values using object names
- Use built-in R functions with the correct basic syntax
- Use the combine function (c()) to group multiple numeric or character values into a single vector
- Describe the structure of a data frame and create one by combining vectors
- Use the $ operator to select a column from a data frame and apply functions to it
- Identify the main data types used in R
- Install and load R packages
- Troubleshoot some common coding errors
:::

**Structure of the session**

Set-up, followed by explanations, demos and short tasks to address each learning outcome.

## User interface: pane layout

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
### [{{< fa regular lightbulb >}}]{style="color: #872046;"}  Learning outcome
- Navigate the RStudio interface
:::

RStudio has 4 panes or 'areas' on the screen, each serving a different purpose for working with R code. The image below shows how these panes are laid out within RStudio:

![](../images/panes.png){width="550" style="display:block; margin: 2em auto;"}
The table below explains what each pane is used for:

::: {#geomxxx-table}
| Pane | What it's used for |
|---------------------|---------------------------------------------------|
| Source | The source pane is mainly used for writing and editing R scripts (documents containing code). |
| Console | The Console is where your R code runs and where you can see the results. |
| Environment | The Environment pane has 4 tabs: Environment, History, Connections, and Tutorial. You will mostly use the Environment tab, which displays information about the data and objects you have stored. |
| Output | The output pane has several tabs (Files, Plots, Packages etc.). In these workshops we'll use the packages tab, which lists the R packages installed on your computer (more on packages later), and the plots tab, which displays graphs that you create. |
:::

::: {.callout-note icon="false" collapse="true"}
### [{{< fa info-circle >}}]{style="color: #9e9e9e;"}  You might not see the source pane to begin with

Don't worry if you don't see the Source pane yet - this will appear when you open a new R Script, which we'll do in the next section.
:::

## Creating and saving a script

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
### [{{< fa regular lightbulb >}}]{style="color: #872046;"}  Learning outcome
- Understand the purpose of a script and how to create and save one
:::

**What is a script?**

A script in R is a file where you can write, save, and organise your code. It is similar to a document in Microsoft Word, but instead of containing text, it contains R code.

**Creating a new script**

There are several ways to create a new script in RStudio. The quickest method is to click the white page icon with the green plus sign below the menu bar, then click "R Script":

![](../images/script.png){width="250" style="display:block; margin: 2em auto;"}

A new blank script will open in the source pane:

![](../images/blank_script.png){width="500" style="display:block; margin: 2em auto;"}

**Saving a script**

Saving a script is similar to saving a Microsoft Word document. To save your script, go to <strong>File &gt; Save As...</strong> and choose a location and filename.

You can also save your script using the keyboard shortcut <strong>Ctrl + S</strong> (or <strong>Cmd + S</strong> on a Mac).

If a script contains unsaved changes, its name will appear in red with an asterisk (*) next to it.

::: {.callout-caution icon="false"}
### [{{< fa laptop-code >}}]{style="color: #2E6B4E;"}  Task
- Create a new script and save it in a **dedicated folder** for the R work on this module.
(This folder will be used to store all of your R scripts and data files for these workshops.)
:::

## Writing and running code

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
### [{{< fa regular lightbulb >}}]{style="color: #872046;"}  Learning outcome
- Write and run R code from a script
:::

There are two places where you can write code in R: in a script or in the console. This is demonstrated below using a very simple piece of code: `2 + 3`.

**Writing and running code from a script**

It is generally recommended to write your code in scripts because it can be edited and saved, allowing you to reopen it and run the code again later.

Code can be written directly in the script:

![](../images/code_script.png){width="400" style="display:block; margin: 2em auto;"}

Then to **run a line of code from your script** (i.e. ask R to execute it):

1. Make sure your cursor is clicked somewhere on that line
2. Either:
    - Click the "Run" button within the Source pane (show below)
    - Or press Ctrl + Enter (or Cmd + Enter on a Mac)
    
![](../images/run_code.png){width="600" style="display:block; margin: 2em auto;"} 
    
The code will execute in the console, where you'll see both the code that was run, and the result:

![](../images/console_23.png){width="400" style="display:block; margin: 2em auto;"}

::: {.callout-note icon="false" collapse="true"}
### [{{< fa info-circle >}}]{style="color: #9e9e9e;"}  Running multiple lines of code from a script

To run multiple lines of code from a script, highlight all of the lines you want to run, rather than placing your cursor on a single line. Then run the code as usual, either by clicking the Run button or by pressing Ctrl + Enter.
:::

**Writing and running code in the console**

The second way to write and run R code is directly in the Console. This is generally not recommended, except for quick calculations or testing a piece of code before adding it to your script.

Unlike code written in a script, code entered directly into the Console is not saved automatically, so it can be difficult to find and reuse later.

To write and run code in the console, type your code next to the command prompt (the `>` symbol) and press Enter on your keyboard. The code will run immediately, and any output will be displayed in the Console.

![](../images/console_code.png){width="400" style="display:block; margin: 2em auto;"}


::: {.callout-note icon="false" collapse="true"}
### [{{< fa info-circle >}}]{style="color: #9e9e9e;"}  The command prompt

Whichever method you use to run code, R needs to be ready to accept a command. You can tell that it is ready when the command prompt (`>`) is displayed in the Console:

![](../images/command_prompt.png){width="400" style="display:block; margin: 2em auto;"}

If you see something else instead (such as a `+` prompt or a partially entered command), R is waiting for additional input and won't run new code. To return to the normal command prompt, click in the Console and press Esc on your keyboard.

You should then see the `>` prompt again. 
:::

## Using R as a calculator

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
### [{{< fa regular lightbulb >}}]{style="color: #872046;"}  Learning outcome
- Write R commands to perform simple arithmetic calculations
:::

Although R is a powerful tool for data analysis and statistics, at its most basic it can be used like a normal calculator. Performing simple calculations is a useful way to start practising writing and running code.

In the previous section, we ran the simple command `2 + 3`. The `+` symbol is an example of an **operator**. Operators tell R to perform a particular action.

One type of operator is arithmetic operators. These are the operators used for everyday mathematical calculations, such as addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division:

::: {#geomxxx-table}
| Action | Operator |
|---------------------|---------------------------------------------------|
| Addition | `+` |
| Subtraction | `-` |
| Multiplication | `*` |
| Division | `/` |
:::

::: {style="margin-top: 2em;"}
:::

We'll come across some other operators through the workshops.

::: {style="margin-top: 2em;"}
:::

:::: {.callout-caution icon="false"}
### [{{< fa laptop-code >}}]{style="color: #2E6B4E;"}  Task
Practise running some more simple calculations based on our three penguins:

- Add together the body masses of penguin 1 (3750) and penguin 2 (4500)
- Use a division to find penguin 1's body mass (3750g) in kg

Run each calculation twice: once from your script and once directly in the Console.

::: {.callout-caution icon="false" collapse="true"}
### [{{< fa magnifying-glass >}}]{style="color: #2E6B4E;"} Answer

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Add together the body masses of penguin 1 (3750) and penguin 2 (4500)
3750 + 4500

# Use a division to find penguin 1's body mass (3750g) in kg
3750/1000
```
:::

::: {style="margin-top: 0.1em;"}
:::

::::

## Adding comments to a script

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
### [{{< fa regular lightbulb >}}]{style="color: #872046;"}  Learning outcome
- Understand the purpose of comments and how to write them in R
:::

In R, a comment is a line of text that begins with a hash symbol (#).

```{r}
# This is a comment
```

In RStudio, comments are displayed in green, making them easy to distinguish from your code.

![](../images/command_prompt.png){width="400" style="display:block; margin: 2em auto;"}

Comments are ignored when the code is executed and do not produce any output. They are used to add notes to your code, such as section headers, explanations of what the code does, make a note of results or add annotations about decisions.

Comments can be placed on their own line or after code on the same line:

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Addition
3 + 6   # the answer is 9
```

As your scripts become longer and more complex, comments become increasingly important. It's a good idea to get in the habit of using them to help explain what different sections of the code are doing, making it easier for both you and others to read, understand, and modify the code in the future.

::: {style="margin-top: 2em;"}
:::

:::: {.callout-caution icon="false"}
### [{{< fa laptop-code >}}]{style="color: #2E6B4E;"}  Task
Add a couple of comments to your script e.g. a title / section heading / note about the calculations.

::: {.callout-caution icon="false" collapse="true"}
### [{{< fa magnifying-glass >}}]{style="color: #2E6B4E;"} Answer

Example:

```{r}
#| eval: false
# R WORKSHOP 1

# Simple addition 
2 + 3

# Add the body masses of penguin 1 and penguin 2
3750 + 4500

# Find penguin 1's body mass in kg
3750/1000
```
:::

::: {style="margin-top: 0.1em;"}
:::

::::

::: {style="margin-top: 2em;"}
:::

## Expressions vs. assignments

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
### [{{< fa regular lightbulb >}}]{style="color: #872046;"}  Learning outcome
- Distinguish between expressions and assignments
:::

**Expressions**

An expression is a piece of code that R evaluates to produce a result. For example, earlier we ran the following code:

```{r}
2 + 3    # this is an expression, which returns the value 5
```

The expression produces a result (`5`), which is displayed in the console but is not saved for later use. 

**Assignments**

Assignments *store* the result of an expression so that it can be used later.

We do this using the assignment operator, a symbol (`<-`) which takes the result of the expression to its right and stores it in an object with the name shown on its left (i.e. it *assigns* that name to the result).

::: {.panel-tabset .panel-blue}
## Template code - assignment

```{r}
#| eval: false
_______________ <- ______________
 object name         expression
```

Let's break this down:

- Fill in the `expression` blank with an expression (the piece of code you want R to run)
- `<-` is called the assignment operator. This operator takes the result of the expression to its right, and assigns the result to the name on its left.
- Fill in the `object name` blank with the name you want to give to the result
:::

For example:

```{r}
x <- 2 + 3  # assigns the result of 2 + 3 to an object called x 
```

::: {style="margin-top: 2em;"}
:::

::: {.callout-note icon="false" collapse="true"}
### [{{< fa info-circle >}}]{style="color: #9e9e9e;"}  Can I use `=` instead of `<-` for assignments?

In R, both `<-` and `=` can be used to assign values to objects. For example, both lines of code below do the same thing.

```{r}
#| eval: false
x <- 2 + 3
x = 2 + 3
```

However, we recommend using `<-` for assignments.

Using `<-` makes your code easier to read because it clearly distinguishes assignment from the use of `=` inside functions.
:::

::: {style="margin-top: 2em;"}
:::

**Assigned objects**

Whenever you assign something to a named object, that object will appear in the Environment tab of the Environment pane:

![](../images/vars_env.png){width="400" style="display:block; margin: 2em auto;"}
You can also view an object by simply running its name. For example, typing and running the code `x` will print whatever is stored in it (in our case, `5`).

```{r}
x
```

**Why are assignments useful?**

At the moment this might seem a bit pointless. Why do we want to save `2 + 3` in an object called `x`?

However, assignments become much more useful when we are working with larger calculations, datasets, and statistical analyses. By assigning a result to a name, we can refer to it again later without having to retype or recalculate it.

You'll see the assignment operator (`<-`) used throughout these sessions, as it is one of the main ways that we store and work with information in R.

::: callout-important
### Write code in your script, not the console

From now on, unless you're testing a small piece of code, write all of your code in the script rather than the console. This makes it easier to save, review, and rerun your work later.
:::

:::: {.callout-caution icon="false"}
### [{{< fa laptop-code >}}]{style="color: #2E6B4E;"}  Task
- Calculate `3 - 2` and store the result in an object named `y`.
- Type and run the object name (`y`) to see the value which is stored in it.

::: {.callout-caution icon="false" collapse="true"}
### [{{< fa magnifying-glass >}}]{style="color: #2E6B4E;"} Answer

```{r}
# Calculate 3 - 2 and store the result in an object named y
y <- 3-2

# Type and run the object name to to see the value which is stored in it
y
```
:::

::: {style="margin-top: 0.1em;"}
:::

## Assigning numeric vs. character values

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
### [{{< fa regular lightbulb >}}]{style="color: #872046;"}  Learning outcome
- Use the correct syntax to assign numeric vs. character values to objects
:::

In the previous section, the expressions that we assigned involved calculations:

```{r}
x <- 2 + 3
```

However, expressions do not have to be calculations. Sometimes we simply want to store a value so that we can refer to it later.

Let's explore this using our penguin data. 

**Assigning numeric values**

When assigning numeric values, we simply type the numbers we want to store.

For example, let's create an object called `mass_1` which stores the body mass of penguin 1 (3750g):

```{r}
mass_1 <- 3750
```

**Assigning character values**

When assigning character values (i.e. text), we need to use quotes around the values.

For example, let's create an object called `species_1` which stores the species of penguin 1 (Adelie):

```{r}
species_1 <- "Adelie"
```

:::: {.callout-caution icon="false"}
### [{{< fa laptop-code >}}]{style="color: #2E6B4E;"}  Task
- As shown above, create an object called `mass_1` which contains the body mass of penguin 1 (`3750`)
- Create an object called `mass_2` which contains the body mass of penguin 2 (`4500`)
- Create an object called `mass_3` which contains the body mass of penguin 3 (`3500`)
- As shown above, create an object called `species_1` which contains the species of penguin 1 (`Adelie`)
- Create an object called `species_2` which contains the species of penguin 2 (`Gentoo`)
- Create an object called `species_3` which contains the species of penguin 3 (`Chinstrap`)

Check all of these objects appears in the environment pane.

::: {.callout-caution icon="false" collapse="true"}
### [{{< fa magnifying-glass >}}]{style="color: #2E6B4E;"} Answer

```{r}
# Create objects containing the three penguin body masses
mass_1 <- 3750
mass_2 <- 4500
mass_3 <- 3500

# Create objects containing the three penguin species
species_1 <- "Adelie"
species_2 <- "Gentoo"
species_3 <- "Chinstrap"
```
:::

::: {style="margin-top: 0.1em;"}
:::

::::

::: {style="margin-top: 2em;"}
:::

## Using stored objects

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
### [{{< fa regular lightbulb >}}]{style="color: #872046;"}  Learning outcome
- Refer to stored values using object names
:::

We have said that assigning values to objects allows you to use them later. Now let's see what that means in practice. Once a value has been stored in a named object, you can refer to it simply by using the object's name. Whenever R sees an object name, it retrieves and uses whatever has been stored in that object.

For example, let's say we want to add the three penguin body masses.

Instead of using the raw values:

```{r}
3750 + 4500 + 3500
```

...we can write the same expression using the names of the objects that store those values, to produce the same result:

```{r}
mass_1 + mass_2 + mass_3
```

As with any expression, we can store its result in a new object. For example, we could store the total of the three masses as "total_mass":

```{r}
total_mass <- mass_1 + mass_2 + mass_3
total_mass  
```

The benefit may not be obvious in such a small example, but storing values in named objects becomes increasingly useful as datasets and calculations become more complex.

::: {.callout-important collapse="true"}
### Be careful not to overwrite your objects

If you assign a new value to an object that already exists, the original contents will be replaced.

For example:

```{r}
#| eval: false
mass_4 <- 3200
mass_4 <- 3350
```
After the second line runs, mass_4 will contain 3350. The original value (3200) will be lost.

If you overwrite an object by mistake, you will usually need to rerun the code that created it in order to restore its original contents:

```{r}
#| eval: false
mass_4 <- 3200
```
:::

:::: {.callout-caution icon="false"}
### [{{< fa laptop-code >}}]{style="color: #2E6B4E;"}  Task
The mass of each penguin is currently given in grams.

- Use your `mass_1` object to calculate the mass of penguin 1 in kilograms

::: {.callout-caution icon="false" collapse="true"}
### [{{< fa magnifying-glass >}}]{style="color: #2E6B4E;"} Answer

```{r}
# Calculate the mass of penguin 1 in kilograms using mass_1
mass_1/1000
```
:::

::: {style="margin-top: 0.1em;"}
:::

## Functions

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
### [{{< fa regular lightbulb >}}]{style="color: #872046;"}  Learning outcome
- Use built-in R functions with the correct basic syntax
:::

You may already have encountered functions in software such as Excel. For example, the SUM() function is used to add values together. Functions in R follow the same general idea.

A function is a block of code that carries out a specific task. This could be something simple, like finding the average of a set of numbers, or something more complex, like creating a graph.

R contains lots of built-in functions that are ready to use. Although each function is made up of code, you do not need to see or understand that code to use it. Instead, you simply use the function's name and provide any information it needs to complete the task.

### A simple example

We saw earlier that we can type and run the name of an object to see what is stored in it. For example:

```{r}
x       # print the information stored in the object called x
mass_1  # print the information stored in the object called mass_1
```

**The print function**

We could alternatively use the `print` function, a function which tells R to display a value in the console.

If you type `print()` and place the name of an object inside the brackets, R will display the value stored in that object. This is another way of viewing an object's contents, and gives the same result as typing the object name by itself.

```{r}
print(x)       # print the information stored in the object x
print(mass_1)  # print the information stored in the object mass_1
```

This is a simple example of a function. R provides many other functions that can be used to perform a wide range of tasks.

:::: {.callout-caution icon="false"}
### [{{< fa laptop-code >}}]{style="color: #2E6B4E;"}  Task

Type and run the following commands (do they all work?):

- `print(species_1)`
- `print(Species_2)`
- `Print(mass_1)`

::: {.callout-caution icon="false" collapse="true"}
### [{{< fa magnifying-glass >}}]{style="color: #2E6B4E;"} Answer

```{r}
#| eval: false
# This will print the value stored in species_1
print(species_1) 

# This will give an error message
# R is case-sensitive, so 'Species_2' and 'species_2' are treated as different
print(Species_2) 

# This will give an error message - the 'p' in 'print' should be lower case
Print(mass_1)    
```
:::

::: {style="margin-top: 0.1em;"}
:::

::::

::: {.callout-note icon="false" collapse="true"}
### [{{< fa info-circle >}}]{style="color: #9e9e9e;"}  R is case sensitive
R is case sensitive — it distinguishes between uppercase and lowercase letters in object and function names. If you see a "not found" error, double-check your spelling and capitalisation.

![](../images/case_sensitive.png){width="400" style="display:block; margin: 2em auto;"}
:::

### General function syntax

Functions follow a general structure: the function name, followed by its inputs - called **arguments** - in brackets. For example, in `print(species_1)`, `print` is the function name and `species_1` is the argument - the object we want to print.

Arguments are the inputs a function needs to carry out a task. Different functions require different arguments - some take just one, while others take several, separated by commas. What you provide depends on the function and what you want it to do.

This structure is shown in the template code below:

::: {.panel-tabset .panel-blue}
## Template code - functions
```{r}
#| eval: false
# Using a function with one argument:
  
________________(______________)
 function_name     argument

# Using a function with more than one argument (put commas between the arguments):
 
 ________________(________________, ________________, ________________ ...)
 function_name     first argument    second argument   third argument


```

- The `function_name` blank should be filled in with the name of the function you want to use.
- The `argument` blank(s) should be filled in with the information that you want the function to work with. If there are multiple arguments, they are separated by commas.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R
Examples of functions:
```{r}
#| eval: false
print(mass_1)           # this prints the value stored within the mass_1 object
class(mass_1)           # this displays the type (class) of data stored in mass_1
sum(mass_1, mass_2)     # this adds the values of mass_1 and mass_2 together
```
:::

```{r}

class(species_1)

sum(mass_1,mass_2,mass_3)
```
:::

## Vectors

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
### [{{< fa regular lightbulb >}}]{style="color: #872046;"}  Learning outcome
- Use the combine function (c()) to group multiple numeric or character values into a single vector
:::

So far, we've been storing single values. A vector is another type of data structure in R that stores an ordered collection of values of the same type. This is more practical when working with lots of values.

To create a vector, we use the `c()` function - the `c` stands for "combine". This is an example of a function with multiple arguments, where each value we want to include is supplied as a separate argument, separated by commas.

This general code structure is shown in the template code below:

::: {.panel-tabset .panel-blue}
## Template code - creating a vector
```{r}
#| eval: false
_______________ <- c(_____________, _______________, ______________ ...)
 object name         first value     second value     third value
```

- Replace the first blank (`object name`) with the name you want to give your vector
- Replace the remaining blanks with the values you want to include in the vector, separated by commas
:::

::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
### [{{< fa info-circle >}}]{style="color: #9e9e9e;"}  Vector rules
- All values in a vector must be of the same type (e.g. all numeric or all character)
- Character values must be wrapped in quotation marks
:::

**Examples**

Rather than storing each penguin's body mass in a separate object, we can store all the values together in a single vector:

```{r}
body_mass_g <- c(3750, 4500, 3500)
```

Notice that we use the assignment operator again to store the vector in an object called `body_mass_g`.

Now let's create a vector of the penguins` species. Just as with single character values, each value must be wrapped in quotation marks:

```{r}
species <- c("Adelie","Gentoo","Chinstrap")
```


:::: {.callout-caution icon="false"}
### [{{< fa laptop-code >}}]{style="color: #2E6B4E;"}  Task
- Create the two vectors `body_mass_g` and `species` as shown in the examples above
- Use the `print` function to print each vector to the console to check it looks as you expect

::: {.callout-caution icon="false" collapse="true"}
### [{{< fa magnifying-glass >}}]{style="color: #2E6B4E;"} Answer

```{r}
# Create vectors called body_mass_g and species containing the body masses and
# species of the three penguins
body_mass_g <- c(3750, 4500, 3500)
species <- c("Adelie","Gentoo","Chinstrap")

# Print each vector to the console
print(body_mass_g)
print(species)
```
:::

::: {style="margin-top: 0.1em;"}
:::

## Data frames

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
### [{{< fa regular lightbulb >}}]{style="color: #872046;"}  Learning outcome
- Describe the structure of a data frame and create one by combining vectors.
:::

A data frame is another type of data structure in R. Unlike vectors, which store a single collection of values, a data frame has a tabular structure - organised into rows and columns. Each row represents a single observation, and each column represents a variable. Data frames are useful because they keep all related information organised together in one place, making it easier to work with and analyse the data.

For example, below is a data frame containing our penguin data. Each row represents a single penguin, with columns recording its species and body mass: 

```{r}
#| echo: false
penguins <- data.frame(species, body_mass_g)
penguins
```

Next, we'll see how to create this data frame.

**Creating a data frame from vectors**

Data frames can be created by combining vectors, where each vector becomes a column in the data frame.

We already have two vectors containing our penguin data - `species` and `body_mass_g`. Rather than keeping them separate, we can combine them into a single data frame so that all of our penguin information is stored together:

```{r}
penguins <- data.frame(species, body_mass_g)
```

This is similar to how we created vectors using `c()` — but instead of combining individual values, we are combining vectors. The arguments are the names of the vectors we want to include, and will form the columns of the data frame.

::: {.callout-important collapse="true"}
### Rules for combining vectors into a data frame
- All vectors must be the same length (i.e contain the same number of values)
- The order of values must match across vectors - for example, the species and body mass for the first penguin should both be in position 1 of their respective vectors
:::

Let's print the data frame to see what it looks like:

```{r}
print(penguins)
```

::: {.callout-note icon="false" collapse="true"}
### [{{< fa info-circle >}}]{style="color: #9e9e9e;"}  Data frames will appear in the environment pane - click to view them
As with other objects, stored data frames will appear in the environment pane, but under "Data".

To view a data frame in the source pane, click on the data frame name (i.e. "penguins" here).

![](../images/env_peng.png){width="400" style="display:block; margin: 2em auto;"}

The data frame will open in a new tab. To return to your script, either close the tab by clicking the "x", or click directly on the script tab.

![](../images/peng_source.png){width="400" style="display:block; margin: 2em auto;"}
:::

:::: {.callout-caution icon="false"}

- Click on the data frame name ("penguins") from within the Environment tab to open it in the source pane.

:::

## Data frames - accessing columns

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
### [{{< fa regular lightbulb >}}]{style="color: #872046;"}  Learning outcome
- Use the $ operator to select a column from a data frame and apply functions to it
:::

It is common to want to work with, or analyse, a specific variable (column) in a data frame.

To access a specific column in a data frame, use the `$` operator. Write the name of the data frame, followed by `$`, followed by the name of the column. For example:

```{r}
penguins$species      # access the species column of the penguins data frame
penguins$body_mass_g  # access the body_mass_g column of the penguins data frame
```

Each column in a data frame is a vector. This means that once you have selected a column, you can apply functions to it just as you did with vectors earlier. For example:

```{r}
print(penguins$species)
```

Earlier, we used the `+` operator to add the three body masses together one at a time. A more convenient approach is to use the `sum()` function on the body mass column:

```{r}
sum(penguins$body_mass_g)
```


:::: {.callout-caution icon="false"}

- Use the `class()` function to find the class (i.e. data type) of the `body_mass_g` column of your `penguins` data frame

::: {.callout-caution icon="false" collapse="true"}
### [{{< fa magnifying-glass >}}]{style="color: #2E6B4E;"} Answer

```{r}
# Print the body_mass_g column of the penguins data frame
print(penguins$body_mass_g)

# Find the class of the body_mass_g column of the penguins data frame
class(penguins$body_mass_g)
```
:::

::: {style="margin-top: 0.1em;"}
:::

## Types of data

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
### [{{< fa regular lightbulb >}}]{style="color: #872046;"}  Learning outcome
- Identify the main data types used in R
:::

We've already seen that R can store both numeric values (such as 3750) and character values (such as "Adelie"). More generally, R represents different kinds of data using different data types.

The three main data types we will encounter in these workshops are:

- numeric – numbers!
- character – text (or numbers stored as text)
- factor – categorical data with a fixed set of possible values

There are a couple of functions we can use to check data types:

- `class()`– Use this function to check the class of an object. For simple objects such as values and vectors, the class usually corresponds to the data type.

- `str()` – Use this function to view the structure of an object. For example, when applied to a data frame, it shows information about each column, including its data type.

:::: {.callout-caution icon="false"}

- the whole `penguins` data frame
- the `species` column only

::: {.callout-caution icon="false" collapse="true"}
### [{{< fa magnifying-glass >}}]{style="color: #2E6B4E;"} Answer

```{r}
# View the structure of the whole penguins data frame
str(penguins)

# View the structure of the species column of the penguins data frame
str(penguins$species)
```
:::

::: {style="margin-top: 0.1em;"}

## Installing and loading packages

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
### [{{< fa regular lightbulb >}}]{style="color: #872046;"}  Learning outcome
- Install and load R packages
:::

An R package is a collection of pre-written functions and other resources that add new tools and capabilities to your R session. Before you can use a package, it must be *installed* on your computer and *loaded* into your current R session.

Think of a package like an app on your phone:

- Installing a package is like downloading and installing an app. You only need to do this once.
- Loading a package is like opening the app so that you can use it. You need to do this each time you start a new R session.

There are three common situations:

- Some standard packages come pre-installed *and* loaded
- Some packages come pre-installed but need to be loaded
- Additional packages need to be installed and then loaded

**Code for installing and loading a package**

To install a package, use the `install.packages()` function. The argument (what you put inside the brackets) is the name of the package you want to install, and needs to be inside quotation marks.

Once a package has been installed, use the `library()` function to load it into your current R session. The argument is the name of the package you want to load, this time *not* in quotation marks.

This is shown in the template code below.

::: {.panel-tabset .panel-blue}
## Template code - installing and loading a package

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| results: hide
install.packages("______________")
                   package name

library(________________)
         package name

```
:::

For example, the following code installs, then loads a package called `Hmisc`:

```{r}
#| eval: false
install.packages(Hmisc)
library(Hmisc)
```

After a package has been loaded, you can use the functions it contains. For example, the `Hmisc` package provides the `describe()` function, which can be used to view a detailed summary of a dataset.

**Warning messages**

You may see some warnings or messages while a package is being installed. This is normal and does not necessarily indicate a problem. 
If the package installs successfully, you should see a message similar to the below:

![](../images/package_ready.png){width="600" style="display:block; margin: 2em auto;"}
You may also see a warning message when loading a package. This is often just R telling you that the package was built using an older version of R. If the package loads successfully, there is usually no need to worry.

If R says that a package "cannot be found", it may not have been installed yet. In that case, run `install.packages()` first, then try `library()` again. Also check spelling and capitalisation of the package name.

**Checking a package is ready to use**

You can check that a package has been loaded successfully by looking in the Packages tab of the Output pane. All installed packages appear in the list. Packages that are currently loaded into your R session have a tick in the box next to their name.

![](../images/tick_Hmisc.png){width="600" style="display:block; margin: 2em auto;"}

::: {style="margin-top: 2em;"}
:::

In the next two workshops, we will use a range of packages to perform additional tasks in R.

::: {style="margin-top: 2em;"}
:::

## Extension: Exploring a data frame

Have a go at using some of the functions below to explore the `penguins` data frame in more detail.

::: {style="margin-top: 2em;"}
:::

| Task | Code |
|------|------|
| Find the number of columns | `ncol(penguins)` |
| Find the number of rows | `nrow(penguins)` |
| Select a single column (variable) | `penguins$species` |
| Look at the first few rows of data | `head(penguins)` |
| Look at the structure of the data | `str(penguins)` |
| Count the number of each species | `table(penguins$species)` |
| Find the mean body mass | `mean(penguins$body_mass_g)` |
| Find the minimum body mass | `min(penguins$body_mass_g)` |
| Generate basic summary statistics | `summary(penguins)` |
| Generate more detailed summary statistics | `describe(penguins)`* |

*the describe function is contained within the Hmisc package (which we installed in the previous section). Therefore, this function will only run properly if you have the Hmisc package installed and loaded.

::: {style="margin-top: 2em;"}
:::

With such a small dataset, some of these functions are not very useful. For example, we can easily see that the data frame contains 3 rows and 2 columns just by looking at it. However, when working with larger datasets containing hundreds or thousands of rows, functions that summarise the structure and contents of a data frame become extremely useful.

In the next workshop, we'll continue to look at functions for exploring and summarising data frames and their columns.

## Summary

In this session, we have learned the basics of using R and RStudio, including how to write and run code, store information in objects, and work with functions.

Part of the session involved creating vectors and data frames from scratch. Although you may not often create data frames manually in this way when working with real datasets, it is a useful exercise for understanding how data frames are structured and for practising key R skills such as assignments, functions, vectors, and data types.

Below is a summary of the main concepts covered in this workshop.

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" collapse="true"}
### [{{< fa regular lightbulb >}}]{style="color: #872046;"} General key points

- R is a programming language for data analysis and statistics. RStudio provides a user-friendly interface for working with R.
- It is good practice to write code in an **R script** rather than directly in the Console, as scripts can be saved, edited and reused.
- The **Source** pane is used for writing code, the **Console** is where code runs, the **Environment** shows objects you have created, and the **Output** pane contains tabs such as Plots and Packages.
- R can be used as a calculator using arithmetic operators such as `+`, `-`, `*` and `/`.
- Comments begin with `#` and are ignored when code is run. They help make code easier to read and understand.
- An **expression** produces a result. An **assignment** stores a result in an object using the assignment operator `<-`.
- Numeric values are written without quotation marks, while character values must be enclosed in quotation marks.
- Once a value has been assigned to an object, you can refer to it later using the object's name.
- Functions perform specific tasks. Functions are called using the syntax `function_name(arguments)`.
- R is **case sensitive**, so spelling and capitalisation matter.
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" collapse="true"}
### [{{< fa regular lightbulb >}}]{style="color: #872046;"} Vectors

- The `c()` function combines values together.
- A **vector** stores multiple values of the same type in a single object.
- Vectors can contain numeric values or character values, but all values in a vector must be of the same type.
- The `c()` function is widely used in R and is useful for creating vectors and supplying multiple values to functions.
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" collapse="true"}
### [{{< fa regular lightbulb >}}]{style="color: #872046;"} Data frames

- A **data frame** stores data in rows and columns.
- Each row represents an observation and each column represents a variable.
- Data frames can be created by combining vectors using the `data.frame()` function.
- When creating a data frame, all vectors must contain the same number of values.
- Each column of a data frame is itself a vector.
- Use the `$` operator to access a column from a data frame, e.g. `penguins$body_mass_g`.
- Functions can be applied directly to data frame columns because columns are vectors.
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" collapse="true"}
### [{{< fa regular lightbulb >}}]{style="color: #872046;"} Data types

- The main data types encountered in these workshops are:
  - **numeric** (numbers)
  - **character** (text)
  - **factor** (categorical data)
- Use `class()` to check the class (type) of an object.
- Use `str()` to view the structure of an object and the data types it contains.
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" collapse="true"}
### [{{< fa regular lightbulb >}}]{style="color: #872046;"} Packages

- An R package is a collection of pre-written functions and other resources that add tools and capabilities to R.
- Before a package can be used, it must be installed and loaded.
- **Install once, load each session.**
- Use `install.packages()` to install a package and `library()` to load it.
- Loaded packages have a tick next to their name in the **Packages** tab.
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" collapse="true"}
### [{{< fa regular lightbulb >}}]{style="color: #872046;"} Troubleshooting tips

- Check spelling and capitalisation carefully.
- Character values need quotation marks.
- Make sure object and column names match exactly.
- If an error message tells you a package or function "cannot be found", check it is installed and loaded. Also check the spelling and capilisation.
- If R is not responding as expected, check that the normal Console prompt (`>`) is displayed.
:::
